HEEWON STYLE — a KOREAN WEBTOON movie still PAINTED like a premium digital painting, the look of a dramatic manhwa cover. A 2:1 movie frame composed for a 2:1 letterbox crop (nothing important at the top or bottom edge). The shot the scene names (wide establishing, two-shot, close-up, over-the-shoulder) from a dramatic camera angle (low three-quarter, worm's-eye, high overhead or dutch), never a flat straight-on catalogue pose. Named characters' FACES are drawn exactly like the attached character sheet: the same clean confident ink linework and manhwa face design (eye shape, brows, nose, jaw, hairline and hair), recognisably those characters, in the clothes the scene gives them. EVERYTHING ELSE IS PAINTED: visible textured brushwork — loose digital-paint strokes and dry-brush, charcoal-like hatching that follow every fold of the silk and every plate of armour, the shadows built from layered strokes, the brightest ridges laid in with single confident strokes, a faint paper-and-canvas grain; at the edges of the garments the linework breaks into loose sketchy strokes. NOT flat cel-shading, NOT smooth airbrushed gradients, NOT a clean vector look, NOT photoreal, NOT 3D. Morning on a long road north through autumn hills after the fall of Great Gaya. Low three-quarter FRONT view: Muryuk rides TOWARD the camera at the tail of a Silla column, alone, tall Gaya cone helm on, steel lamellar under a dusty dark travel coat with a purple sash, rocking with his horse, eyes fixed forward and down on the road ahead of him, jaw set, lost in thought; he does NOT turn his head. Far BEHIND him, over his shoulder on a distant ridge, a thin smoke smudge where Gaya was, which he is not looking at. Plain blank blue Silla pennants on poles at the frame edge, no emblems or marks on them. The road is one long diagonal into misty hills. Low gold morning sun rakes across his face and the grass. Most of the frame is quiet sky and hill. CHARACTER SHEET, left to right: LEFT face = muryuk. Copy each face exactly; give each person the dress the scene names. KIM MURYUK — Look: Square weathered Gaya face, heavy brows, long pauses in the eyes; grows grey, then white, but never bald under the helm. Dress: Out of battle: plain dark Gaya-cut po with a purple sash; the tall Gaya cone helm (고깔 투구, iron plates, small crest) on his head or under his arm, ALWAYS, even indoors at home (it sits on a stand by the door at night). Now: Greying, then grey-bearded; the cone helm still on. Colour #8B5CF6. BACKGROUND AND LIGHT (painterly tenebrism): the background IS the place and the moment of the scene — open sky if they are in the sky, the hall if they are in a hall, the gate, the river, the snow — painted loosely in atmospheric brushwork (drifting smoke, cloud, haze, mist, falling snow, embers) in the scene's own colours, soft and out of focus, with a faint bokeh of small lights; it has colour, weather and depth — never a flat black void, never a detailed set; crowds and armies only as massed painted shapes dissolving into haze. ONE hard directional key light that belongs to the place (a brazier, a lamp, the sun through cloud, a torch, moonlight) rakes across the faces and clothes from the side or from below, modelling them in high contrast with deep painted shadows and a thin edge of the same light along the silhouette. Each character's colour lives in that light and in the atmosphere around them — never a glow aura or halo. Faces and bodies act the beat: real expressions, real weight, mid-motion. Faces from the sheet; new poses, never the sheet's stance. Each named person appears once, never cloned. Everyone wears period clothing of their own court (Korean, Tang, Yamato, Mohe furs), never European dress. No text, no speech bubbles, no panel borders, no watermark.
